lead: A dynamometer is a brake that measures the torque it absorbs. The engine turns, the dynamometer resists, and a torque arm and load cell turn that resistance into a number. A test cell is the room built around that brake: rigid bed, guarded coupling, fuel and coolant lines, exhaust extraction, fire safety and a panel that logs speed, torque, temperatures and flows. Together they make an engine measurement repeatable and safe. Every brake power figure in the other chapters comes from a dynamometer.
prereq: You need: brake power from torque and speed in the chapter on measuring indicated, brake and friction power, and bmep in the chapter on performance parameters.

blocks.text: A dynamometer must do two things: take the engine's power, and measure the torque. Dynamometers fall into three groups.

items: Absorption dynamometers turn the power into heat and measure the reaction torque: the Prony brake, the rope brake, the hydraulic (water) brake and the eddy-current brake.

Transmission dynamometers sit in the drive line and measure the torque while the power passes on to the load, from the twist of a shaft or from strain gauges on a torque flange; they absorb almost nothing.
Driving (motoring) dynamometers are electric machines that can absorb power as a generator and also drive the engine as a motor: the swinging-field DC machine and the AC machine.

blocks.text: In the Prony brake a lined block is clamped on the flywheel and a lever carries the reaction to a spring balance. Torque is force times perpendicular distance: T = W × L, where W is the net force on the arm in N (reading minus the zero reading) and L is the arm length from the shaft centre in m. In the rope brake a rope is wrapped round the flywheel rim with a dead load W hanging on one end and a spring balance reading S on the other. Then T = (W − S) × R<sub>e</sub>, where R<sub>e</sub> = (D + d)/2 is the effective radius, D the drum diameter and d the rope diameter.

blocks.where: BP is brake power in W; N is engine speed in rev/min; T is torque in N·m. Divide by 1000 for kW.

items: Prony and rope brakes: cheap and simple, but the grip changes as they heat, they need water cooling and they suit only small engines at low speed.
Hydraulic brake: a rotor churns water inside a casing mounted on trunnions; the water level sets the load, and the casing reaction on a torque arm gives T. It suits large powers.

Eddy-current brake: a toothed rotor turns in the field of coils, and eddy currents drag on it; the coil current sets the load, so it changes quickly and smoothly. Cooling water carries the heat away. It can only absorb.
Swinging-field DC machine: the field casing sits on trunnions and its reaction torque is read on an arm; as a generator it absorbs power into a resistor bank, as a motor it drives the engine.

blocks.text: An absorption brake can only load the engine. A motoring dynamometer is an electric machine that can also drive the engine. A DC machine motoring at controlled speed gives the motoring test: the engine is turned without fuel, and the shaft power needed equals friction power (see the chapter on measuring indicated, brake and friction power). The same machine can generate, so one unit covers both directions.

A transient dynamometer goes further. It changes speed and torque fast enough to follow a driving cycle second by second. An AC dynamometer uses a vector-controlled induction or synchronous machine with low inertia. It works in four quadrants: forward motoring, forward generating, reverse motoring, reverse generating. That lets it reproduce a stop-start city pattern, a cold start, or a turbo lag event.

An absorption dynamometer cannot do this. It cannot motor the engine, so it cannot follow the overrun (engine-braking) parts of a cycle, and friction and water brakes respond too slowly to follow a prescribed speed-torque trace. An eddy-current brake responds fast but still only absorbs.

sections.h3: The test cell makes the measurement repeatable

blocks.text: A test cell is a room designed around the dynamometer. The engine sits on a rigid bed, often on anti-vibration mounts, aligned to the dynamometer shaft. The coupling between engine and dynamometer carries a fixed guard: a spinning shaft at 5000 rev/min must never be exposed.

Services are fixed: fuel supply with a measured tank or flow meter (see the chapter on fuel and air measurement), coolant circuit with a heat exchanger and temperature control, ventilation to supply combustion air and remove fumes, exhaust extraction to carry gases outside, and fire detection with a clean-agent extinguisher.
The instrument panel logs speed, torque, temperatures and flows at the same time. Repeatability comes from keeping all of these the same from run to run.

items: Warm the engine to a steady coolant temperature.
Set the speed and load on the dynamometer controller.
Log torque, speed, fuel flow and temperatures together.
Repeat the point once to check drift.

spec.aria: Engine shaft driving a rotor inside a swinging casing; a 0.5 metre arm presses a load cell with 120 newtons; torque 60 newton metres and brake power 9.42 kilowatts.

examples.question: A hydraulic dynamometer has a torque arm of 0.5 m. At 1500 rev/min the spring balance reads 120 N. The engine is a 1.0 L four-stroke. Find the torque, the brake power and the bmep.
steps: Torque: T = W × L = 120 N × 0.5 m = 60 N·m.
Angular speed: ω = 2πN/60 = 2π × 1500 ÷ 60 = 157.08 rad/s. Brake power: BP = T × ω = 60 × 157.08 = 9425 W = 9.42 kW.
Swept volume: V<sub>d</sub> = 1.0 L = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³; a four-stroke has n<sub>R</sub> = 2.
bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub> = 2π × 2 × 60 ÷ (1.0 × 10⁻³) = 7.54 × 10⁵ Pa = 7.54 bar.
examples.answer: T = 60 N·m, BP = 9.42 kW, bmep = 7.54 bar.
examples.check:
import math
W = 120.0
L = 0.5
N = 1500.0
V<sub>d</sub> = 1.0e-3
n<sub>R</sub> = 2
T = W * L
BP = 2 * math.pi * N * T / 60
bmep = 2 * math.pi * n<sub>R</sub> * T / V<sub>d</sub>
print(round(T, 2))
print(round(BP / 1000, 2))
print(round(bmep / 1e5, 2))

examples.question: A rope brake is fitted to a flywheel of diameter 1.0 m with a rope of diameter 20 mm. At 600 rev/min the dead load is 300 N and the spring balance reads 50 N. Find the torque and the brake power.

traps: Using the drum diameter as the arm of a rope brake. The arm is the effective radius (D + d)/2, 0.51 m in worked example 2, not 1.0 m.
Forgetting the zero reading of a torque-arm balance, or adding the spring reading in a rope brake. The net force is the reading minus the zero, or W − S.
Dropping the 60. With N in rev/min, BP = 2πNT/60; leaving out the 60 makes the power 60 times too large. With ω in rad/s, use BP = Tω.
Mixing mm and m. A 500 mm arm is 0.5 m, not 500.
Confusing bmep with brake power. bmep is pressure, in bar or Pa; BP is power, in kW.

quiz.q: What does a dynamometer measure directly: torque, power or speed?
quiz.a: Torque. Power is computed from torque and speed.

quiz.q: Why does a Prony brake lose accuracy at high speed?
quiz.a: Friction heat fades the lining, the block or rope loses grip, water cooling becomes uneven, and the arm vibrates.

quiz.q: A torque arm of 0.4 m carries 80 N at 2000 rev/min. Find T and BP.
Why can an absorption dynamometer not follow a city driving cycle?
quiz.a: It cannot drive the engine during the overrun and closed-throttle parts of a cycle, and friction and water brakes cannot change load fast enough to follow a speed-torque trace second by second.

quiz.q: A rope brake carries a dead load of 90 N, and the spring balance reads 10 N; the effective radius is 0.5 m. At 1800 rev/min, find T and BP.
Classify dynamometers and give one example of each.
quiz.a: Absorption (Prony, rope, hydraulic, eddy-current), transmission (torsion shaft, torque flange) and driving or motoring (swinging-field DC machine, AC dynamometer). Only the driving type can turn the engine without fuel.

quiz.q: Why is the coupling guard a safety requirement, not an option?
quiz.a: The shaft spins at high speed. A hand, sleeve or cable can be caught in the coupling; the guard keeps people and loose items away.

quiz.q: Write the bmep formula and define n<sub>R</sub>.
quiz.a: bmep = 2π n<sub>R</sub> T / V<sub>d</sub>. n<sub>R</sub> is 2 for a four-stroke engine and 1 for a two-stroke engine.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production engine plants use AC transient dynamometers with automated test sequences, and electric vehicle motors are tested on the same beds with regenerative absorption. Research cells add in-cylinder pressure logging and fast emissions benches. Search for 'transient dynamometer driving cycle' and 'AC dynamometer four quadrant'.
